statement: The cued base's loop hazard at T 0.6 is a property of the problem rather than of its own text so far: under truncated low-temperature sampling a stuck model locks into a repeat at a roughly steady rate per token (2610.24715), so problems whose solutions must run long (the hard ones, long for RL too) collect the loops, early zlib compressibility predicts loops only across problems because those problems produce well-compressing enumerations and case lists, and RL's prefix helps because it carries the solution further, not because it is less self-similar.
why_strongest: Each measured value is a comparison across problems, so a problem-level hazard explains all three. Test k2 (AUROC 0.67) compares loopers with non-loopers on different problems, and hard, long problems both compress better early and loop more. Test k3 (0.63) compares base and RL openings, which differ in style for reasons unrelated to looping. The best-controlled test, k4, compares problems inside the 78-problem pool, which is already uniformly hard. There compressibility nearly stops predicting cap hits: 0.56, against the theory's 0.66. That fall is what a difficulty hazard predicts and a self-reinforcement mechanism does not. The account also fits the board items the theory lists as conflicts. Excess cap hits sit in RL's longest quartile (knowledge-9e4147). The base's cap-hit problems are the long ones for RL too (result-5de032). Restarts recover only part of them, and K_fresh still caps on about half (knowledge-1497e8). The lock theorem in 2610.24715 and the low-temperature, learned-error account of looping in 2512.12895 supply the per-token mechanism without any dose-response on the history.

tests.experiment: Within one problem, cued base at T 0.6 / top-p 0.95: is the opening of a sample that hit the cap more compressible than the opening of a fresh restart of the same problem that finished?
tests.recipe: Files s3://pg-lineage-769063704696/results/rlneurons/r4/modal_k-01/k_b/K_fresh.jsonl (rln4_gen rows) and s3://pg-lineage-769063704696/results/rlneurons/r3/base-01/out/F_math500.jsonl (rln3_gen rows). Define ratio(s) = len(zlib.compress(s.encode('utf-8'), 9)) / len(s.encode('utf-8')) (Python zlib, level 9). For each problem_index in K_fresh, take its K_fresh row; if there are several, take the one with the lowest sample. Keep the problem only if that K row has cap_hit false, len(text) >= 3000, and not (loop_A true with onset_A_char missing or < 3000). Its partner F row is the F_math500 row with the same problem_index and cap_hit true; if there are several, take the lowest sample. Drop the problem if there is no such F row, if len(F.text) < 3000, or if ratio(F.text[:8000]) < 0.10. For each kept problem compute rF = ratio(F.text[:3000]) and rK = ratio(K.text[:3000]). Score 1 if rF < rK, 0.5 if they are equal, else 0. Statistic: mean score over kept problems. Report the number of kept problems.
tests.theory_should_say: The theory says the capped sample's own history was already more self-similar, as its own within-problem prediction puts it, so it should give about 0.62-0.65. The rival says the hazard is fixed by the problem, so two samples of the same problem have equally compressible openings, about 0.5.

tests.experiment: Does problem difficulty, measured by RL's answer length on the same problem, predict a later rule-A loop in the cued base at T 0.6 / top-p 1.0, on the same rows where early compressibility was tested?
tests.recipe: Files iterate-runs:abaybektursun-1114-151718-d4fa/answers.jsonl (run_cell rows, base cue, T 0.6 / top-p 1.0) and s3://pg-lineage-769063704696/results/rlneurons/r3/s2800-01/out/P_math500.jsonl (rln3_gen rows, RL step 2,800, plain). From the d4fa file, keep rows with len(text) >= 6000 characters that either have loop_A false or have loop_A true with onset_A_char >= 7000; drop rows with loop_A true and onset_A_char missing or < 7000. Join each kept row by problem_index to the P_math500 row with sample == 0; drop rows with no such RL row. Score each kept row with d = the RL row's n_generated; RL cap hits keep their n_generated as stored. Statistic: AUROC of d as a score for loop_A == true (Mann-Whitney form, ties count 0.5). Report the number of kept rows and positives.
tests.theory_should_say: The theory holds that difficulty acts on the loop hazard only through the self-similarity of the base's own text, so a proxy measured on another model's answer should predict no better than the base's own compressibility, about 0.6-0.67. The rival makes difficulty the direct cause, so it predicts clearly better, about 0.72.

tests.experiment: Does early compressibility still predict a rule-A loop once problems are matched on difficulty (AUROC computed within quartiles of RL answer length)?
tests.recipe: Files iterate-runs:abaybektursun-1114-151718-d4fa/answers.jsonl and s3://pg-lineage-769063704696/results/rlneurons/r3/s2800-01/out/P_math500.jsonl. From d4fa, keep rows with len(text) >= 6000 characters that either have loop_A false or have loop_A true with onset_A_char >= 7000 (drop loop_A true with onset_A_char missing or < 7000). Join each kept row by problem_index to the P_math500 row with sample == 0; drop rows with no such RL row. For each kept row compute s = len(zlib.compress(text[:6000].encode('utf-8'), 9)) / len(text[:6000].encode('utf-8')) and d = the RL row's n_generated. Compute q1, q2, q3 = numpy.percentile(d over kept rows, [25, 50, 75]) (default linear interpolation). Stratum 1 = d <= q1, 2 = q1 < d <= q2, 3 = q2 < d <= q3, 4 = d > q3. Within each stratum, form every pair of one row with loop_A true and one row with loop_A false; a pair scores 1 if s_pos < s_neg, 0.5 if they are equal, else 0. Statistic: total score over all within-stratum pairs divided by the total number of within-stratum pairs (a stratum with no positives or no negatives contributes nothing). Report the number of pairs and positives per stratum.
tests.theory_should_say: The theory makes self-similarity the proximate cause, so compressibility should keep its predictive power among problems of equal difficulty, about 0.65, close to the unstratified 0.67. The rival says most of that 0.67 comes from mixing easy and hard problems, so it should fall toward 0.5, about 0.57.
